---
title: "Exercise: camera noise, SNR and PSNR"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- compute **shot noise** and the SNR of a pixel, and what averaging frames gains,
- judge from a camera's **full well**, **read noise** and **ADC bits** how many bits carry information,
- say when the **additive Gaussian** noise model is reasonable,
- compute a **PSNR**, and explain why the peak must be stated.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked *(math)* are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

## By hand

**B1.** A camera has a full well of 15 000 electrons, a read noise of 3 electrons, and a 12-bit ADC whose range is matched to the full well.
(a) What is the gain (electrons per ADU)?
(b) What is the dynamic range, as a ratio, in dB ($20\log_{10}$) and in bits?
(c) Is 12 bits enough? Compare one ADU with the read noise.

**B2.** One pixel collects on average 400 electrons, another 40 000. Give the shot noise and the SNR of each. You average 4 frames of the dim pixel: what happens to its SNR, and why?

**B3.** Noise model. For each case, is "additive Gaussian noise with one $\sigma_n$ for the whole image" a reasonable model? (a) A dark-field image: almost all pixels near 5 electrons, read noise 3 electrons. (b) A fluorescence image with a background of 50 electrons and nuclei of 20 000 electrons. (c) A photo saved as a strongly compressed JPEG.

**B4.** An 8-bit image is corrupted by Gaussian noise with $\sigma_n = 5$ grey levels.
(a) What are the MSE and the PSNR (peak 255)?
(b) A denoiser halves the noise SD. What is the new PSNR, and by how many dB did it improve?

**B5.** A 12-bit camera image (values 0…4095) has noise of 80 ADU; it is saved in a 16-bit file. One paper reports its PSNR with peak 4095, another with peak 65 535. Compute both. Which one is right?

**B6.** The dim pixel of B2 (400 electrons) also has 3 electrons of read noise. What is its SNR in one frame? How many frames must you average to reach an SNR of at least 50?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) $g = 15\,000 / 4095 \approx 3.66$ electrons per ADU. (b) $15\,000/3 = 5000 : 1$, which is $20\log_{10}5000 \approx 74.0$ dB, or $\log_2 5000 \approx 12.3$ bits. (c) Just about. One ADU (3.66 electrons) is a little larger than the read noise (3 electrons), so the quantisation noise $3.66/\sqrt{12} \approx 1.06$ electrons is not negligible. Added in variance it raises the dark noise from 3 to $\sqrt{3^2 + 1.06^2} \approx 3.18$ electrons, about 6 % more. A 13-bit ADC would make one ADU smaller than the read noise.

**B2.** Shot noise $\sqrt{400} = 20$ and $\sqrt{40\,000} = 200$ electrons; SNR $400/20 = 20$ and $40\,000/200 = 200$. 100 times more light gives 10 times the SNR. Averaging 4 frames of the dim pixel is like collecting 4 times the light (1600 electrons, noise 40): the SNR doubles, to 40. Averaging only helps because the noise differs from frame to frame.

**B3.** (a) Reasonable: read noise is close to Gaussian and, at a nearly constant 5 electrons, the shot noise ($\sqrt5 \approx 2.2$) is about the same everywhere; total $\sigma_n \approx \sqrt{5 + 9} \approx 3.7$ electrons. (b) Not with one $\sigma_n$: the shot noise is about $\sqrt{50} \approx 7$ electrons in the background and $\sqrt{20\,000} \approx 141$ in the nuclei. Gaussian within each region, but with a signal-dependent $\sigma_n$. (c) No: compression errors depend on the image content and are correlated between neighbouring pixels (blocks), not independent.

**B4.** (a) MSE $= \sigma_n^2 = 25$, PSNR $= 10\log_{10}(255^2/25) = 34.2$ dB. (b) $\sigma_n = 2.5$: MSE $6.25$, PSNR $= 40.2$ dB, an improvement of $20\log_{10}2 = 6.0$ dB.

**B5.** Peak 4095: $10\log_{10}(4095^2/80^2) = 34.2$ dB. Peak 65 535: $58.3$ dB, 24.1 dB more for the same image. The peak should be the largest value the **data** can take, 4095 here; the container (16-bit file) does not matter. Only PSNRs computed with the same peak can be compared.

**B6.** Noise $\sqrt{400 + 3^2} = \sqrt{409} \approx 20.2$ electrons, SNR $= 400/20.2 \approx 19.8$ (25.9 dB), a little below the pure shot-noise value 20. Averaging $n$ frames multiplies the SNR by $\sqrt n$: $19.8\sqrt n \ge 50$ needs $n \ge 6.4$, so **7 frames**.
:::

### Math questions

**B7.** *(math)* With shot noise, read noise $\sigma_r$ and quantisation (gain $g$) independent, the total noise is $\sigma^2 = S + \sigma_r^2 + g^2/12$. For the camera of B1, compute $\sigma$ at $S = 100$ electrons. Above which signal does shot noise dominate the read noise? Show that the best possible SNR is $\sqrt{N_\text{max}}$ (ignore read and quantisation noise at the full well).

**B8.** *(math)* Show that rounding to $b$ bits (step 1 on the scale $0 \dots 2^b - 1$, error uniform) gives $\text{PSNR} = 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) + 10\log_{10}12$, and evaluate it for $b = 4$ and $b = 8$.

**B9.** *(math)* $K_1, \dots, K_n$ are independent Poisson counts with mean $N$. Show that their average has mean $N$ and variance $N/n$, and express the gain in SNR in dB.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B7.** $\sigma = \sqrt{100 + 9 + 1.06^2} \approx 10.5$ electrons. Shot noise exceeds read noise when $\sqrt S > \sigma_r$, i.e. $S > \sigma_r^2 = 9$ electrons. At the full well the noise is $\sqrt{N_\text{max}}$, so $\text{SNR} = N_\text{max}/\sqrt{N_\text{max}} = \sqrt{N_\text{max}}$: about 122 for 15 000 electrons.

**B8.** The error is uniform on $[-\tfrac12, \tfrac12]$, so MSE $= 1/12$ (quantisation unit). PSNR $= 10\log_{10}\big((2^b - 1)^2 \cdot 12\big) = 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) + 10\log_{10}12$. For $b = 4$: $23.52 + 10.79 = 34.3$ dB; for $b = 8$: $48.13 + 10.79 = 58.9$ dB.

**B9.** $\mathbb E[\bar K] = \frac1n\sum\mathbb E[K_i] = N$; by independence $\operatorname{Var}(\bar K) = \frac1{n^2}\sum\operatorname{Var}(K_i) = \frac{nN}{n^2} = \frac Nn$. The SNR is $N/\sqrt{N/n} = \sqrt{nN}$, $\sqrt n$ times that of one frame: $20\log_{10}\sqrt n = 10\log_{10}n$ dB (6.0 dB for 4 frames).
:::

## Explore {#explore}

A simulated camera images the micrograph. The plot shows noise against signal, in electrons: shot noise, read noise, quantisation noise, their total, and points measured on simulated flat patches.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="camerabits" data-fwc="30000" data-read="1.5" data-bits="16" data-exposure="0.5"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/camerabits.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Preset **sCMOS 16 bit**. How large is one ADU in electrons, and the quantisation noise? Which noise source dominates in the dark, and which in the bright? Do the measured points follow the model?

**E2.** **Same, 8-bit ADC**. What happens to the gain and the quantisation noise? Why are the measured points for dark patches drawn as red triangles (measured noise 0)? Is zero noise good news here?

**E3.** Compare **low light, 8 bit** and **low light, 12 bit**: how many different ADU values does the image use, and what do you see?

**E4.** **Noisy, 16-bit ADC**: how many ADU is the read noise? How many bits does the readout say are needed? What do the other bits store?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** One ADU is $30\,000/65\,535 \approx 0.46$ electrons, and the quantisation noise $0.13$ electrons, far below the read noise of 1.5. In the dark the read noise dominates (the flat blue line), above a few electrons the shot noise $\sqrt S$ takes over. The points sit on the total curve (e.g. 9.89 measured against 10.11 predicted at 100 electrons). The last point, at the full well, falls below: saturated pixels are all equal, so they have no noise left.

**E2.** One ADU is now about 118 electrons and the quantisation noise 34 electrons, far above the read noise. In a dark flat patch the true noise (a few electrons) is much smaller than one ADU, so every pixel rounds to the same number: the measured spread is 0. That is not good news. The signal differences below one ADU are not noisy, they are gone. The model $g/\sqrt{12}$ also fails at 1000 electrons (measured about 59, predicted 46): it assumes the signal varies over many steps.

**E3.** 8 bits: only 4 different values in the image (the brightest pixel is 2.6 ADU), so the cell is a few flat patches. 12 bits: 48 values (brightest 41 ADU); the cell is recognisable, and noisy. In dim light the ADC's step, not the sensor, decides what survives.

**E4.** The read noise is 10 electrons and one ADU is $10\,000/65\,535 \approx 0.15$ electrons, so the read noise is about 66 ADU, around $2^6$. The readout says 10 bits would do ($\log_2 1000 \approx 10$). The lowest ~6 bits of every pixel record read noise very precisely.
:::

## Where this leads

The noise model here, Poisson shot noise plus Gaussian read noise, and the SNR and PSNR defined here are used whenever the course measures noise: **denoising** with smoothness priors and wavelets, **reconstruction** of CT images, **compression**, and choosing exposure times in quantitative microscopy. The next unit is about storing and displaying the 12- and 16-bit numbers such cameras produce.
